en: % NB: ṭarkvi corrected to ṭakki throughout PiKraṬi:

[p. 15] Homage to Vajrasattva! Herein, the sequence of meditation for the *Piṇḍīkrama* composed by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna is indicated according to its actual meditative procedure. First of all, the yogin, seated on a comfortable cushion in a delightful place such as a forest and so forth, beholds all sentient beings who are defiled by the faults of conceptual construction and habitual tendencies. Having brought to mind great compassion, whose essential nature is the desire to deliver them from those states, he proceeds.

Having recited, "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature," and having removed the ordinary ego through the focus on emptiness, one should instantly manifest oneself in the form of Vajrasattva. Having recited "Vajradhṛk," one should emit Akṣobhya from that [form] and cause him to enter into oneself. Having formed a protective armor with the three syllables, one should proceed according to this sequence: "Abiding in the samādhi of Dveṣavajra, one should begin the protection of the site" (7cd).

Then, having emanated the ten wrathful deities from the seed-syllable in the heart of Akṣobhya, and having commanded the second Sumbha with the mantra, and having again given the command with the second mantra, one should nail down the obstacles with that very mantra, Sumbha. Then, outside the stakes, one should visualize walls of iron, water, fire, and wind with the mantra: *Ṭakkir hūṃ jaḥ*. Such is the tradition.

Thereafter, having uttered the syllable *bhrūṃ* and visualized a vajra-fortress in the form of a stūpa arising from its transformation, one should contemplate emptiness by means of the verse beginning with "By nature... and so forth. Then, awakened by great compassion, one should see a bow-shaped wind-maṇḍala born from the syllable *yaṃ*, marked with vajras on its two sides by two *hūṃ* syllables. Likewise, one should visualize the fire, water, and earth maṇḍalas. Having seen the ground as consisting of a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) through the transformation of these, [one proceeds].

Above that, having meditated upon a peaked pavilion (kūṭāgāra) born from the syllable *bhrūṃ*, resting upon a moon disc on a double-lotus (*viśvapadma*), and provided with the wheel-thrones and so forth for the deities of the maṇḍala; and in the center, having seen the three syllables *hūṃ oṃ āḥ* upon a moon disc at the heart of the filaments of a sun, moon, and double-lotus, and having again visualized these three syllables—all this transforming, one instantly emanates oneself in the form of Vajrasattva, surrounded by the thirty-two deities.

Having seen those maṇḍala deities as being absorbed through their essential nature into the aggregates and so forth, one should cause them to enter the ultimate maṇḍala. He demonstrates this with the passage beginning "the aggregate of form" (*rūpaskandha*) and so on. Vairocana has the nature of the mirror-like wisdom. The earth element is Locanā. The eye faculty is Kṣitigarbha. And "form" (*rūpa*) is Rūpavajrā. Maitreya, together with Yamāntaka and Acala, is also included within Vajradhara. The aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*) is the equality-wisdom, Ratnasaṃbhava. The water element is Māmakī.

Now Māmakī is remembered as belonging to the Ratna family; subsequently, she will belong to the Akṣobhya family, wherein there is an obscuration in both families. The auditory faculty is Khagarbha, and Śabdavajrā. Regarding the "two wrathful deities," these are Prajñāntaka and Takkirāja. Perception is the state of discernment (pratyavekṣaṇya), which is Amitābha; Hutabhuj is Pāṇḍaravāsinī. The olfactory faculty is Lokeśa, and Gandhavajrā. Regarding the phrase "accompanied by the two wrathful deities," these are Padmāntaka and Nīladaṇḍa.

The formative factors (*saṃskāra*) are the performance of activities, [represented by] Amoghasiddhi. "Māruta" refers to Tārā. "The sense-faculty of taste" refers to Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin and Rasavajrā. "Endowed with the two wrathful deities" refers to Vighnāntaka and Mahābala. "Joined with the two wrathful deities above and below" refers to Uṣṇīṣa and Śumbha. Mañjughoṣa has the nature of the three gnoses and the nature of the mental faculty (*mana-indriya*); by way of illustration, Vajrapāṇi and Samantabhadra are also to be understood [in this manner].

In this regard, Maitreya and Kṣitigarbha belong to the Vairocana family; Khagarbha belongs to the Ratna family; Lokeśa belongs to the Amitābha family; Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhī belongs to the Amoghasiddhi family; and it should be understood that the remaining three belong to the Akṣobhya family. Then, having recited "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness," one causes Vajrasattva also to enter the clear light by means of the sequence of the mirror and the breath, and thus enters into non-apprehension.

Then, through the impelling force of previous vows (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*), [the seed-syllables] instantly appear and transform into the form of a solar disc; above that, one should visualize a moon, a lotus, and the three syllables. Having transformed all of these into the moon, and from the moon, a white vajra produced from the three syllables; and from the vajra, Mahāvajradhara. One should contemplate the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the entry of Akṣobhya. Therein, having performed the placement of the syllables *oṃ*, *āḥ*, *hūṃ*, *svā*, and *hā* on the head and other parts.

Having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) of *lāṃ*, *māṃ*, *yāṃ*, *tāṃ*, *brūṃ*, *śaṃ*, *gaṃ*, and *syaṃ* upon the elements beginning with earth; having placed *thīṃ*, *oṃ*, *oṃ*, *oṃ*, *hūṃ*, *ūṃ*, *maiṃ*, and *saṃ* upon the eyes and other sense organs; and having placed the ten *hūṃ*s of Yamāntaka and the others upon the arms and so forth—therein, Yamāntaka and Aparājita are on the right and left arms; Hayagrīva is in the mouth; Amṛtakuṇḍalin is in the secret place; Acala and Ṭakkirāja are on the right and left upper arms; and Nīladaṇḍa and Mahābala are on the right and left knees.

One should place Uṣṇīṣacakravartin upon the head and Sumbharāja at the feet. Then, having performed the empowerment of body, speech, and mind, one should place the Jñānasattva—two-armed, red in color, holding a vajra and a vajra-bell, and in union—within the heart of the Samayasattva. Within his heart, one should place the syllable HŪṂ, known as the Samādhisattva. Thereafter, having purified the aggregates and so forth of an external consort (bāhyāṅganā) belonging to the washerman family, or of a Jñānamudrā, and having performed the consecration of the vajra and lotus;

One should perform the meditative union with those two. Therein, by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, one should visualize a five-pronged vajra; on its central prong, the syllable *praṇava* (*oṃ*). By means of the syllable *āḥ*, one should contemplate an eight-petaled lotus of red color in the center of the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*). This is the consecration of the vajra and the lotus. Through the sequence of kissing and embracing, one should arouse passion with the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) of Ratnasambhava. In the state of the bodhicitta [at the moment of its emission], one should assume the ego-identity of Amoghasiddhi.

Then, from that *bodhicitta*, by means of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) of the arising of Wisdom (*prajñā*) within the lotus of Wisdom, one should instantly emit the mandala-circle consisting of the thirty-two deities. Thereafter, from the secret mandala, one should purify the external emission mandala with the mantra beginning with "Vajradhṛk" and so forth, emanating it individually; having thus effected the purification of the hatred and other afflictions of sentient beings and adorned them, one should contemplate them seated sequentially in the form of the aforementioned mandala-circle.

However, one should visualize that in the center, within the nature of the central Vajradhara, the Dveṣavajra has entered; and within the nature of Sparśavajra, one should visualize that Sparśavajrā has entered. Alternatively, this may be done by recollecting the seed-syllables such as *HŪṂ*. Then, one should instantly visualize the entry of the wisdom-circle (*jñānacakra*), the consecration, the act of passion, and so forth.

Then, having performed the vajra-recitation and so forth, preceded by exhortation, praise, and the like, one should cause sentient beings to enter the syllable *hūṃ* by uttering *hūṃ*, [those beings] being of the nature of the samādhi-sattva; then one should dissolve the members of the maṇḍala. In that very place, one should dwell while beholding the Viśvavajrasattva produced from that. Thus ends the *Piṇḍīkramatippaṇī*.
